extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical geometry and surveying (historical)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and propositions for measuring areas (including circle segments and figures on slopes) and for dividing triangles/figures into equal parts using geometric constructions and proportional arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between arc, chord, and corresponding proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements about the proportional relations linking an arc of a circle, its chord, and quantities derived by multiplying by diameter/semidiameter (e.g. proportions of arc to whole circle correspond to numbers made from half-diameter and circumference measures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiplicative proportionality: multiply arc-related limits by diameters (or vice versa) to translate arc measures into comparable numerical quantities for further arithmetic (summing, dividing). The text repeatedly prescribes multiplying arc limits by chosen numbers to get comparable measures (e.g. to compare arcs, chords, and portions cut from a circle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute area of a figure composed of a triangle plus a circular portion
rubrics_metrics.description: To measure an area made of a triangle together with an adjacent circle-portion, find the area of the triangle and add the area of the circular portion (each measured separately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate and compute the area of each simple component (triangle, circular sector/segment) and sum them. The passage explicitly prescribes decomposing a composite figure into known parts, measuring each, and adding their areas to obtain the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring a plane figure on a slope by projection (surveying with a pertica and plumb)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a field lies on the slope of a hill and you must measure its surface, project it to a horizontal plane by constructing perpendiculars and equidistant lines using a rod (pertica) and a plumb bob (archipendolo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: fix a pertica, use the plumb to drop perpendiculars to a reference line, mark successive points so that the pertica is equidistant to that reference, trace lines parallel/equidistant to obtain a planar representation. Then measure the projected planar figure as usual. The text gives two practical modes (one using repeated placements of a rod and plumb to trace equidistant lines; another using an instrument that suspends a line with a plumb) and notes these are the standard surveying ways to reduce sloped surfaces to planar measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a triangle into two equal-area parts through a given vertex or midpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: If dividing a triangle into two equal areas by a line from a vertex, draw the line to the midpoint of the opposite side; conversely, lines through a midpoint to the opposite vertex split the triangle equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the required dividing line must pass through a vertex and bisect the opposite side, the two resulting triangles are equal in area. The text shows this standard construction and uses proportionality of similar triangles to justify equality of areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a triangle into two equal parts through an arbitrary interior point (non-midpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the given point inside the triangle is not on the median, construct a line through the point that divides the triangle into two equal areas by using proportional constructions: multiply appropriate sides/segments and extract required lengths (including taking square roots) to locate the dividing line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text prescribes arithmetic steps (multiplication of side lengths, forming squares, extracting roots) to compute the required position of the cutting line when the simple median construction does not apply. It gives numerical-algorithm style instructions (multiply, take roots, divide) to find the point on the opposite side such that the line through the given interior point yields equal areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a triangle into n equal-area parts (thirds, fourths, etc.) using proportional partitions and parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: To partition a triangle into multiple equal-area parts, divide one side into the required number of proportional segments and draw parallels (or use repeated similar-triangle constructions) so that the resulting bands/triangles are equal in area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text demonstrates dividing a triangle into two, three, four, or more equal parts by successive proportional divisions of sides and by constructing parallels or similar triangles. It prescribes multiplying side lengths by appropriate integers and using the resulting proportional segments to generate the equal-area divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using similar triangles and proportionality to transfer area ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: When triangles have equal altitudes or share angles, their areas are in proportion to corresponding bases; similarly, corresponding segments in similar triangles are proportional and these proportions can be used to deduce equal-area or proportional-area constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book repeatedly invokes the proportionality of sides in similar triangles and the proportionality of areas to bases when altitudes are equal. Use these relationships to construct lines that preserve or produce desired area ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing lines equidistant/equidistant-to-a-line using plumb and rod
rubrics_metrics.description: To create a line equidistant to a given line (or to reproduce a given offset at a distant location on sloped terrain), use a rod and plumb to transfer perpendicular distances and trace the equidistant locus point by point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: place the rod at successive stations, suspend plumb to mark perpendicular foots on the reference, use the sequence of marked points to trace the equidistant line; repeat until the desired parallel/equidistant line is completed. This is presented as the field technique for surveying sloped figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposing complicated planar figures into triangles/quadrilaterals to compute area
rubrics_metrics.description: A complicated figure's area can be found by decomposing it into triangles (or quadrilaterals) whose areas are computable, then summing or subtracting these component areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text prescribes dividing figures into a finite set of simpler polygons (triangles, quadrilaterals), measuring each (via known constructions or proportional calculations), and combining results arithmetically. It emphasizes selecting decompositions into parts proportional in a manageable way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic operations as part of geometric constructions (multiply, divide, root extraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many geometric constructions and area-division tasks are reduced to explicit arithmetic operations: multiplying segment lengths by integers, dividing by integers, forming squares, and taking square roots to obtain required construction lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manuscript gives step-by-step recipes: e.g., multiply given side by certain integers, add/subtract products, form squares and extract roots to find a length whose placement as a segment yields the desired proportional division of area. These arithmetic instructions are integral to performing nontrivial divisions of areas in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a point inside a triangle yields unequal partitions by angle-drawn lines, locate dividing lines by balancing area via proportional constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: When lines drawn from an internal point to vertices produce unequal area partitions, construct auxiliary parallels or use proportional multiplications to find lines from that point that balance the areas as required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains how to handle cases where the obvious angular or median constructions do not produce equal areas: use proportional reasoning on adjacent sides/segments, multiply and divide to compute the correct intercept point on a side, then draw the line from the given interior point to that intercept to achieve equal-area division.
